newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian villagers ambush marauding gunmen.
newsitem.headline: Albanian villagers ambush marauding gunmen.

text.p: A bloody shootout between Albanian villagers and a roving gang of gunmen left 20 people dead in this central hamlet in the worst violence since state authority collapsed this month, witnesses said on Friday.
They said five cars ferried some 25 gunmen into the village 110 kms (65 miles) south of Tirana on Thursday. The men, some wearing masks, fired rounds into the air and shouted insults.
"Hand over your weapons, you sons of bitches," one villager quoted a gunman as screaming.
Two villagers came towards the gunmen and were shot dead, witnesses said. The spots where the men fell in the lone street are marked by white rocks, candles and a vase with flowers.
One man, Frad Selimi, 28, was gunned down just outside his home. Women wailed inside on Friday where his body was laid out with a rose placed in his mouth ahead of burial.
While the gunmen blasted away in broad daylight, villagers took up positions in crumbling buildings overlooking the street and then rained down automatic arms fire.
A long streak of blood and oil lines the street where most of the gunmen were cut down from the rooftops. But some ran to the nearby cars to try to flee.

"Some pleaded for their lives. One offered money to be spared but it was too late," a villager said. In the end, 17 gunmen were killed and one was badly wounded. Three villagers died in the shooting, witnesses and the local morgue said.
Outlaw gangs have roamed Albania with impunity since police and military authority collapsed this month in the face of a popular uprising. Jails were opened and criminals fled.
Thousands of Albanians stormed army munitions depots and seized huge quantities of weapons, throwing large parts of the country into anarchy and lawlessness.
The uprising began as a challenge to rightest President Sali Berisha over his handling of failed investment schemes in January, which wiped out the savings of many Albanians.
Frakull's mostly gypsy population joined in the wholescale theft of weapons. "We looted the guns to protect ourselves. We have a right to protect ourselves," another villager said.
A score of men had set up barricades at the entrance to the village and nervously fidgeted with Kalashnikov assault rifles, some fixed with bayonets. Machineguns were set on rooftops.
No motive for the incident has been given. Police have not returned to the village since overseeing the evacuation of the bodies in private cars and on an armoured personnel carrier.
Villagers accused the gunmen variously of being secret police, bandits or just plain thugs out to fighten a gypsy village. Everyone was nervous and bracing for reprisals.
Some families left the village. A family of nine gypsies walked passed. One carried a Kalashnikov, another a baby and the rest sacks of food, pots or personal items in blankets.
In the nearby town of Fier, police said a number of the men came from the region and funerals took place throughout the day to bury the dead.
A large crowd showed up for the funeral of Nebi Backa, 28, described as a businessman by his family.
"So far nobody knows the real motive for what was going on. They went there to meet at a nearby club and have coffee with friends," said Backa's uncle, Il Backa, 37.
Backa said he blamed the village for what had happened.
"You can't kill people like animals. Maybe one or two but not all of them," he said.

Backa said his nephew and the other men had gathered from towns around the region "to settle some scores with people from Gjirokaster", well to the south near the Greek border. He gave no other details.
Asked if he thought his nephew's death would be avenged, he said: "We need only time. It's clear in a country where nothing is functioning that something must be done by us."
